result.killer: No single killer. Partial substitute: the ODPC's own free online registration portal, with links pushed to the email addresses entities registered at PACRA, ZRA and the Registrar of Societies (Afriwise roadmap). I found no evidence of enforcement against micro firms by October 2026.
result.reason: I found nothing that kills it outright. There is no Zambian product, association tool or packaged service for micro-business registration and renewal, and no exemption or deferral. The duty is real: a yearly certificate under the micro tier (up to 10 staff), with the 30 April 2025 deadline. The demand is weak, though. The regulator's own online portal does the core job: one annual form, with registration links sent to each entity's registered email at PACRA or ZRA. I found no 2026 enforcement, audits, fines or registration counts. I couldn't check the micro fee (Second Schedule; ZambiaLII returns 403), and it is probably small. Willingness to pay for help with a simple yearly form looks low. Score lowered from 4 to 3.

result.killer: No single killer was found. Risks are timing and market size. The Act was still uncommenced as of 5 August 2026 (ZambiaLII, per Global Law Experts), and BoZ has issued no return templates. Existing licences remain valid until expiry (per Africa-Legal commentary, not checked against the Act text). BoZ's existing BSA/IISS returns channel already serves licensed non-bank institutions. Capital and governance requirements may make small lenders leave the market instead of licensing. Not verified: whether Intelligrow (a Lusaka Mifos/Fineract implementer), Voxforem or Bravelender export BoZ returns.
result.reason: Nothing kills it outright, but it is premature and the market is thin. Act No. 9 of 2026 was assented to on 31 March 2026. ZambiaLII still listed it as uncommenced on 5 August 2026. I found no commencement statutory instrument, no BoZ transition circular and no return templates. Existing licences stay valid until expiry. BoZ already runs its own submission channel for non-bank institutions (Bank Supervision Application / IISS, plus email). Licensed non-bank institutions already file there, so the new part of the market is ex-moneylenders. Minimum capital and governance rules (compliance officer, internal audit) may push small informal lenders out rather than into licensing. Not verified: Voxforem, Bravelender, Intelligrow (a Mifos implementer) or Lendsqr exporting BoZ returns. I found no count of moneylenders.

coverage.category: 1. Household employers: domestic workers, live-in carers, nannies
coverage.found: Domestic workers are covered by the Employment Code (Domestic Workers Minimum Wages and Conditions of Employment) Order, 2023 (cited by WageIndicator; the wage figures were not confirmed). NAPSA registers employers and domestic workers through eNAPSA, which has a domestic-worker section; contributions are 5% employer plus 5% employee. Payroll returns are already rejected (K07). Weak household-employer candidate listed.

coverage.category: 2. Scrap-metal dealers
coverage.found: The Scrap Metal Dealers Act (Cap 409, Ministry of Commerce, Trade and Industry) requires a licence, a register of transactions, holding scrap for 7 days, police search power and cancellation. The licensing authority is the city/municipal/township council or the District Secretary. No 2025/2026 amendment found. Full text not machine-readable, so register contents unverified.

coverage.category: 3. Second-hand dealers and pawnbrokers
coverage.found: The search returned only South African, NZ and Australian regimes. No Zambian second-hand dealer or pawnbroker law found. Pawn lending may fall under Bank of Zambia non-bank lender rules (unverified).

coverage.category: 4. Gold and jewellery buyers
coverage.found: Gold Trade Act 1912 is still listed. Zambia Monitor reports a coming revised framework with separate licences for mining, processing, trading and export of gold, to be issued by a Minerals Regulation Commission, with Bank of Zambia as sole authorised buyer. No bill number or dates. Lusaka Times (July 2026): ZCCM-IH and the Ministry of Mines are discussing gold markets; 700-1,000 cooperatives hold licences.

coverage.category: 5. Used car parts and vehicle dismantlers
coverage.found: Not searched specifically; no search budget was left after the other categories. No evidence found either way. Treat as unchecked.

coverage.category: 6. Livestock traders, markets and animal transport
coverage.found: The Department of Veterinary Services issues stock movement permits and slaughter permits via ZamPortal. Applicants need a ZamPass digital signature, NRC and a lab/vet report. Fees are tiered by species and number (ZMW 20 for 1-4 animals, ZMW 50 for 5-50, per a third-party site). Per-movement permit, so the duty recurs.

coverage.category: 7. Small abattoirs and butchers
coverage.found: Cattle Slaughter (Control) Act permits (inspector-granted) and the ZamPortal slaughter permit (ZMW 100/200 for immature/pregnant animals). No abattoir or butchery licensing details found.

coverage.category: 8. Beekeepers
coverage.found: Animal Health (Bee Keeping) Regulations, SI 94 of 2020, set import/export permits for bee products. The Zambia Residue Control Plan keeps EU honey-export listing. 2025 official push on traceability. CIFOR says no legal structure monitors beekeeping; the date of that statement is unclear.

coverage.category: 9. Veterinary practices and veterinary medicine sellers
coverage.found: The Veterinary and Veterinary Para-Professions Act 2010 (Veterinary Council of Zambia licenses animal health facilities). ZAMRA registers agro-veterinary shops under the Medicines and Allied Substances Act 2013 Part III (certificate, annual returns, display, transfer; class III shops need a VCZ-certified suitably qualified person; guidelines effective Jan 2018). An amendment bill to the 2010 Act is on the Parliament site, status unclear.

coverage.category: 10. Well drillers and water abstraction
coverage.found: SI 18, 19 and 20 of 2018 cover charges/fees, driller licensing and groundwater/borehole regulations (notice of intention to drill, borehole registration, defective borehole reports). WARMA now requires GPS devices on rigs. Covered by known K05.

coverage.category: 11. Septic, sanitation and waste haulers
coverage.found: Solid Waste Regulation and Management Act No. 20 of 2018 (in force 11 April 2019) licenses solid waste service providers, operators and self-service providers, covering collection and transport. Older Cap 204 transporter regulations may still apply. No small-operator specifics, fees or portal found.

coverage.category: 12. Lift, boiler and pressure-equipment owners and inspectors
coverage.found: Factories Act: steam and air receivers must be notified to an inspector before use and examined periodically. SI 8 of 2018 (Plant Inspection and Examination Fees) has the Commissioner notify owners by registered letter 10 days ahead. Nothing found on lifts or on private inspectors.

coverage.category: 13. Small water systems
coverage.found: NWASCO regulates utilities; a 2018 NWASCO rural framework exists. No licensing or return details for community water trusts could be found. NWASCO restored North Western utility licence June 2025 (large utility, not relevant).

coverage.category: 14. Pesticide and fertiliser dealers and applicators
coverage.found: ZEMA Pesticide and Toxic Substance licence (Environmental Management (Licensing) Regulations, SI 12 of 2013) is required to store, distribute or transport pesticides. It needs a local council trading permit, is valid 3 years, takes about 30 days and is applied for on ZamPortal with ZamPass. Add the ZAMRA agro-vet shop registration. Near K04 but a different duty.

coverage.category: 15. Labour contractors and recruitment agencies
coverage.found: The Employment Code Act 2019 provides for registration of employment agencies. The old Cap 268 Part VIII had Labour Commissioner licences with a 30-day court appeal. Which provisions are in force, and the fees and process, were not confirmed.

coverage.category: 16. Cemeteries, burial societies and funeral services
coverage.found: Cemeteries and burial permits run under the Public Health Act Cap 295 and the Local Government Act No. 2 of 2019. Lusaka City Council sells burial permits (K27 in one report) and is short of land (17,717 deaths in 2025). Private cemetery operators exist. No funeral-parlour licensing regime found.

coverage.category: 17. Community and religious bodies: associations, charities, halal and kosher supervision
coverage.found: NGO Act 2009 (amended by Act 13 of 2020) gives a registration board and register. A 2024 NGO bill (annual returns and audit, penalties up to 3 years) had unknown status. Companies limited by guarantee also file PACRA annual returns within 3 months of year-end. Nothing on halal or kosher supervision.

coverage.category: 18. Transport operators: minibus, taxi, moto-taxi, small trucking and bus fleets
coverage.found: RTSA Road Service Licences (Road Traffic (Amendment) Act No. 8 of 2022): the long-term list ran 1 Sep 2023 to 31 Aug 2026, so a new cycle has just started. GPS is mandatory on PSVs. Fitness certificates are periodic (3, 4 or 12 months by class per a third-party site). Night ban 21:00-05:00. E-hailing SI 19 of 2024. RTSA's e-ZamTIS and ZamPass are used. No Zambian operator-side compliance software found.

coverage.category: 19. Market traders, street vendors, money changers
coverage.found: Bank of Zambia Bureau de Change regulations (SI 38 of 2003, with 1998 weekly returns rules and a 2003 circular on capital and annual fees); current rules not confirmed. Market and street traders face ZRA presumptive tax and council or cooperative levies, with a levy dispute at the Lusaka intercity terminus. No obvious software buyer.

coverage.category: 20. Small licensed premises with inspections: tattoo studios, driving schools, childminders and nurseries, small food producers, hunting outfitters
coverage.found: The search returned only South African results for early childhood centres. No Zambian rules found for driving schools or nurseries. Tattoo and hunting not searched. Mark largely unchecked.

result.competitor: Generic loan software that could cover part of the job: Loandisk, Musoni (has built central-bank returns for Zimbabwe, but I found nothing for Zambia), Bravelender (Lusaka loan accounting software), Voxforem, Lendsqr, and the Selar Excel 'Zambia Loan Management Compliance System' (claims unverified). I saw no product producing BoZ returns for ex-moneylenders, but the templates don't exist yet, so the gap can't be confirmed. Local-language search was not applicable because legal and business practice is English-language.
result.duty: Partly confirmed. Act No. 9 of 2026 makes lending as a business a 'financial service' that needs a BoZ licence. Licensees must file periodic prudential returns to BoZ, report to credit-reference bureaux, disclose fees and meet AML/KYC/STR duties. Operating unlicensed is a criminal offence: up to 3m penalty units or 30 years' imprisonment (Zambia Monitor, Africa-Legal). The duty is NOT yet in force. Global Law Experts, citing ZambiaLII as of 5 Aug 2026, says the Act is 'uncommenced' and no commencement order has been gazetted. I found no commencement SI in my searches. Old licences stay valid until they expire. The transition length depends on the commencement order and is unknown. Return frequency and format will be set by future BoZ directives or SIs, which I could not find.
result.market: Not found. There is no published count of Money-lenders Act certificate holders. Gazette notices (e.g. Gazette No. 7566, Mar 2024) list individual applications without totals. I could not open the parliamentary brief (HTTP 503), so the figure of 99 non-deposit-taking institutions is unverified. Advocacy group I-ZAP says almost all online lenders are unlicensed. A 2021 bill debate raised concern that higher licence fees would push small lenders out of the market, which suggests the paying base after licensing may be small.
result.reason: The Banking and Financial Services Act No. 9 of 2026 is real. It repeals the Money-lenders Act Cap. 398 and requires credit-only lenders to hold a BoZ licence. It also brings prudential returns, credit-bureau reporting, fee disclosure and AML/STR duties, with penalties of up to 3m penalty units or 30 years in prison. However, Global Law Experts, citing ZambiaLII on 5 Aug 2026, says the Act is still uncommenced. I found no commencement order and no BoZ return templates or frequency for these lenders. I also found no count of moneylenders. Loandisk, Musoni and Bravelender exist, but I saw none producing BoZ returns. High capital and licensing costs may push many small lenders out, which shrinks the market. This is worth revisiting once commencement and the BoZ directives are published.

coverage.category: 37. Bank of Zambia licensed moneylenders, bureaux de change, mobile money agents
coverage.found: Big change: the Banking and Financial Services Act 2026 (Act No. 9 of 2026, per law-firm commentary and Zambia Monitor; not confirmed against the gazette) repeals the Money-lenders Act Cap. 398 and brings moneylenders under BoZ licensing as financial service providers. Commentary says capital, governance, prudential/periodic returns, credit-bureau reporting, AML/KYC and fee disclosure apply. A commentary page said the Act was uncommenced as of 5 Aug 2026, and no transition window was found (existing licences stay valid until expiry). Bureaux de change: BoZ supervises under the 2003 BDC Regulations; weekly returns are filed by the Monday via the BoZ Bank Supervision Application System, with daily late penalties of K100-1,500 (Circular 01/2022, via the regalert.today aggregator). The market is small and the filing portal is state-run, so it is weak. Mobile money agents: the Agent Banking Directives 2022 and the 2023 E-Money Directives put KYC and registration on the operators (MTN and Airtel; over 150,000 agents per a 2022 article). Nothing found on agent-side compliance duties or a register to keep. Unchecked: current bureau count, the gazetted Act text and commencement, BoZ return templates for non-deposit lenders.

Applications go through the zamportal.gov.zm e-government portal (unverified), and fees are listed on a third-party site only (unverified). Quarry approvals (project brief or EIS) carry conditions on licences, waste disposal, closure and inspector access. Nothing found on recurring annual returns for small firms, and enforcement against small waste haulers looks weak (UNZA studies, UN-Habitat). No local software or service for ZEMA licence tracking was seen. Unchecked: whether licence renewals or annual environmental reports are mandatory and what they cost, and whether the zamportal licence application flow is free and usable.

result.competitor: I found no Zambian product that tracks RSL, fitness or GPS compliance for operators. Fleet GPS vendors operating in Zambia (Frotcom Zambia in Ndola, Ctrack Zambia, Ezytrack, and providers on the GoAfrica directory) advertise tracking, fuel and maintenance, but not licence or fitness expiry reminders. Their generic maintenance-schedule features could probably do this. RTSA's e-ZamTIS on Zamportal already handles online fitness test applications, road tax, registration and PSV driver licence renewal, but not the RSL. A Zambian job ad shows fleet compliance records (registration, insurance, fitness) are still kept by hand. I could not do a full search of the fleet vendors.
result.duty: Real and in force in Zambia. A Road Service Licence (RSL) is required for each PSV and goods operator, valid for 3 years under s.109. RTSA notices give two different cycles: 1 Jul 2023 to 30 Jun 2026 and 1 Sep 2023 to 31 Aug 2026. The application needs a ZRA tax clearance, fitness certificate, insurance, vehicle and driver lists, a speed limiter certificate and proof of GPS fitment. Under s.110B of Road Traffic (Amendment) Act No. 8 of 2022, RTSA can suspend or revoke the licence for breaking its conditions. GPS: SI 78 of 2016 (PSV GPS Regulations) makes a working GPS on PSVs a condition of the RSL. The fine is up to 1,000 penalty units and/or 3 months in jail. Enforcement is real: RTSA suspended the Talwaka Lumo / Emmanuel Kasunga licences for 3 months over an inactive GPS. Roadworthiness (fitness) tests and road tax are recurring duties. I did not confirm how long the fitness certificate is valid. I also found no RTSA notice for the 2026-2029 RSL cycle (not reached).
result.market: Not verified. I found no count of operators or RSLs. CEIC reports about 86,846 vehicles registered in Dec 2023, which looks like new registrations, not the fleet. RTSA de-registered 223,148 inactive vehicles in 2023. RTSA's annual report (2024) would likely have RSL figures, but it returned HTTP 503. RTSA's published applicant lists for the 2023 cycle run to several batches, which suggests thousands of operators, but most are single-vehicle minibus owners.
result.reason: The duties are real and enforced (3-year RSL, GPS condition under SI 78/2016, fitness, road tax), but the core job is mostly a reminder calendar. The heaviest step, the RSL, comes only every 3 years. Fitness tests and road tax are already handled online through e-ZamTIS on Zamportal. GPS is already sold by tracking vendors, who could add expiry alerts cheaply. Buyers are mostly informal owners of one or two minibuses with little willingness to pay, and they would be reached through bus station associations. Larger fleets already pay GPS vendors. A done-for-you RSL renewal service for each cycle might work better than software, but I could not confirm when the 2026 cycle opens. The MVP is simple, but its value is low.

result.competitor: ZamPortal (free state e-services, ZamPass login) handles co-operative services, including registration and cancellation of registration by the Department of Co-operatives, as seen on mabumbe.com mirror listings. Whether co-operative annual returns are filed there is not confirmed: the minister only said the deadline is shown on ZamPortal. The ILO My.Coop package is training, not software. Uganda's state CRMIS is a non-Zambian example. I found no commercial Zambian co-operative compliance software or done-for-you service. The mabumbe.com page that gave me a 403 was not reached.
result.duty: Annual returns from registered co-operatives under the Co-operative Societies Act (Cap 397, 'Yearly and other returns' section) and SI No. 25 of 2024. I did not see the SI text; its content comes from the minister's 31 Aug 2025 statement. The minister said returns are due three months before the end of the calendar year, so around 30 Sept. Persistent defaulters will be deregistered and non-compliant co-operatives are barred from Ministry funding. No fine is reported. I could not confirm the fee or the required attachments for co-operatives. The ZamPortal guidance for the Registrar of Societies (a different registry) lists a 31 March deadline, a K150-250 fee, and attachments of financial report, audited accounts and annual report.
result.market: The minister in 2025 cited about 139,000 registered co-operatives with about 10,000 compliant. The same article's headline says 129,000, so the figures conflict. Coops4dev/Registrar data for 2019 gives 9,498 registered co-operatives with about 1.58m members, which casts doubt on the 139k figure. The government says it loses about K18m a year in fees.
result.reason: The duty is real. The Co-operative Societies Act has a yearly-returns section, and the minister said on 31 Aug 2025 that SI 25 of 2024 makes returns mandatory, with deregistration and loss of Ministry funding for defaulters. I did not open the SI text itself. I found no commercial product. ZamPortal already offers free online filing with ZamPass sign-in, but I only saw its co-operative services through a third-party mirror, so whether co-operatives file annual returns there is unconfirmed. Return form and fee are unconfirmed (the K150-250 fees seen are for societies). The buyers are mostly poor rural co-operatives and only about 7% comply. Willingness to pay is likely low, so the realistic buyers are donors or bookkeeping bureaus. The work is an annual paperwork and accounts job, so the value is in service, not software.

result.competitor: The ODPC online registration portal is free apart from the statutory fee (dataprotection.gov.zm returned 503). Law-firm advisory exists (Bowmans, Afriwise). Generic foreign compliance sites (consentstack) exist but don't file. The World Bank DZAP tender (closed Aug 2026) builds the regulator's own compliance management system, which could simplify the portal. I found no Zambian micro-business registration or renewal service with pricing.
result.duty: Data Protection Act No. 3 of 2021 s20 and the Data Protection (Registration and Licensing) Regulations SI 58 of 2021 require data controllers and processors to register. The Second Schedule sets fee tiers for micro, medium, large and individual. A secondary source says the certificate is valid one year and must be renewed at least 3 months before expiry. The ODPC set 30 April 2025 as the registration deadline, and failing to register is an offence (ZMW 200,000 fine and/or up to 5 years, per Bowmans). Not verified: the micro fee amount (SI page returned 403, PDF unreadable), any deadline extension, and actual enforcement after April 2025.
result.market: Not found: the ODPC has published no count of registered entities. In principle the duty covers almost every formal business that holds personal data in Zambia (tens of thousands of PACRA-registered firms), but I found no statistic. Actual uptake among micro firms is unknown.
result.reason: The duty is real. Data Protection Act No. 3 of 2021 s20 and SI 58/2021 require registration with fees in size tiers, including micro. A secondary source says the certificate lasts one year and renewal is due at least 3 months before expiry. The ODPC portal deadline was 30 Apr 2025, with a ZMW 200,000 fine and/or up to 5 years. I found no local done-for-you or SaaS for micro firms, only law firms (Bowmans, Afriwise) and the ODPC portal. Weaknesses: I found no enforcement evidence after April 2025 and no registration statistics. I couldn't confirm the micro fee. The ODPC site and the SI page were unreachable. The task is a simple yearly form, so willingness to pay is low and churn is high. It works best bundled into a vertical tool or an accountant's service.

result.competitor: There are two sources of competition. First, ZRA Smart Invoice is a free state tool (Windows, Android and web), mandatory since 1 July 2024, and its scope explicitly includes Tourist Tax. Second, Odoo modules certified to connect to ZRA's VSDC already handle the levy: Pokutsoft's l10n_zm_smart_invoice (about $118) maps the 1.5% Tourism Levy to ZRA tax labels and has a POS version, and AminiTech's ZRA POS is about $244. Hotel PMS products sold in Zambia include DJUBO and ResRequest, though I did not confirm whether either integrates with Smart Invoice. I found no product that pre-fills the monthly levy return or tracks ZTA licences, but the return is simple and the licence cycle is only every 3 years.
result.duty: Confirmed and in force. The Tourism and Hospitality (Tourism Levy) Regulations, SI 56 of 2016, started on 1 March 2017 (SI 69/2016) and were amended by SI 121 of 2020 (Reg 8A: 5% penalty on understated levy; collection moved under the VAT Act). The rate is 1.5% of the total bill for accommodation, conference/convention and food and beverages. The levy is remitted to the ZRA Commissioner-General by the 14th of the following month. Returns are due by the 5th if filed manually, or the 14th if filed online. Other penalties: 5% of the unpaid amount per month, and 1,000 penalty units per month for not filing a return. Separately, ZTA licences are renewed every 3 years, and ZTA is pushing 1 to 5 star grading (Lusaka Times, 11 Sep 2026, snippet only). Also not to be confused: SI 100/2016 sets a 10% service charge with a quarterly return to ZTA. I did not check whether this applies to small lodges.
result.market: The only count found is 948 licensed tourism enterprises (Tourism Update, 6 Sep 2018), which covers all types, not just accommodation. ZTA said about 75% of enterprises were compliant. Only 36 establishments were star-graded in April 2025. I found no current register count for small lodges or guest houses. It is likely in the low thousands at most, including unlicensed operators.
result.reason: The duty is real. Under SI 56/2016 as amended by SI 121/2020, the levy is 1.5% of the total bill for accommodation, conferences and food and beverages. It is remitted to ZRA by the 14th of the following month, with a monthly return. Penalties are 5% per month on unpaid levy, 1,000 penalty units per month for missing returns, and 5% on understated amounts. However, ZRA's free Smart Invoice, mandatory since 1 July 2024 with penalties from October 2024, covers Tourist Tax. Cheap Odoo connectors (about $118 to $244) already map the 1.5% Tourism Levy to ZRA tax labels, so the levy is calculated at invoice time and the return is a simple TaxOnline step. Licence renewal every 3 years is too infrequent to need a tracker. The market is small: 948 licensed enterprises (2018 figure).

The duty is not yet in force. The Ministry of Mines PS said the revised framework, with separate mining, processing, trading and export licences, goes to Parliament once it resumes. I found no gold bill. The only 2026 bill found is the MRC (Amendment) Bill N.A.B. 32, which concerns board composition. The claim's "Gold Trade Act 1912 still listed" is doubtful, because a search snippet says the Gold Trade (Repeal) Act 2015 repealed it. The Minerals Regulation Commission Act 14 of 2024 is real and commenced in June 2025. It covers trading licences, so the commission name is confirmed. The government plans single-buyer routing through ZCCM-IH and the Bank of Zambia, which would shrink the private dealer market. No recurring reporting duty is defined, and no competing software was found, though I did not check for any. Market size was not found. Revisit if a bill is gazetted.

The export permit duty is real: SI 94 of 2020 requires a Form I permit from the Director of Veterinary Services to import or export honey or hive products for sale, with a fee. I could not read the PDF text (the fetch returned undecodable binary), so I did not confirm penalties, renewal frequency or any record-keeping clause. No Zambian legal traceability duty was found. The 2025 traceability remark is only a policy statement, and the EU residue plan is a government obligation, not one on small firms. The market is tiny: few exporters, with 853 t produced in 2021. The permit is an occasional, per-consignment filing, so there is little recurring pain. I found no software, but also no sign of demand. SNV traceability work is NGO-led. Low score.

The duty is real. Chilanga Town Council's notice (Lusaka Times, 16 Sep 2026) set an Oct 31, 2026 renewal deadline for 2027 business levies, health permits, fire certificates and petroleum storage permits. Penalties are "as prescribed by law", with no amounts found. The legal basis in the claim is wrong: the Trades Licensing Act was repealed by Act No. 18 of 2011, so the real basis is council by-laws or other business licensing law, which I did not identify. Councils (Chilanga, Lusaka) already have online payment platforms, so the core payment step is covered by the state. A third-party tracker is not shown to exist, but the market is fragmented by council. Willingness to pay is low and a council-by-council MVP is hard to scale. No register count found.

NHIMA accreditation and claims submission are real (NHIMA says it processes provider claims, over 400 accredited providers in 2026). Payment delays and rationing are reported. Carepeak Clinic withdrew from May 2026, and the Healthcare Federation reports over K100m owed. I did not find the claims submission procedure or any provider portal or API. I found no Zambian vendor offering NHIMA claims tools, but that search was thin. A "mandatory recurring duty" is weak: claiming is voluntary billing, not a legal duty. The market is small (about 400 providers, mostly not small clinics), and providers are cash-strapped, so willingness to pay is low. Dependence on NHIMA's undocumented system raises MVP risk. Score stays at 3.

Could not read the Act text (ZambiaLII and LEAP both returned 403). Search snippets say the Controlled Substances Act 2023 commences on a date the Minister appoints by statutory instrument. I found no commencement SI. The licensing and ss32-34 records duties are confirmed only through a LEAP summary. I found no source for the quarterly-return (s11) claim or for penalties. The Medicines and Allied Substances Act 2013 (Part III) does include a pharmacy annual return. I found no pharmacy-register software or competitor, and no count of licensed pharmacies. The market is likely small, a few hundred to low thousands of outlets. The duty may fall on licensed handlers rather than ordinary pharmacies, and payment capacity is low. The score stays at 3.

Act No. 9 of 2026 was assented on 31 March 2026 and repeals the Money-lenders Act. ZambiaLII listed it as uncommenced and I found no commencement order, so the duty is not yet confirmed in force. This rests on a search summary because the ZambiaLII fetch returned 403. Existing licences stay valid until they expire. I found no deadline for moneylenders to relicense, no BoZ return templates and no count of unlicensed lenders. Penalty figures differ between sources. Competitors include Lendsqr, Voxforem, Bravelender, Questbanker and a $98 Excel compliance pack on Selar, so the niche is partly served. Buyers are small and have little willingness to pay. Keep the score low until commencement and a transition window are confirmed.
